1.s: Jacob’s family grows into a great people in Egypt. A new Pharaoh, afraid of them, forces them into slavery and orders their baby boys to be killed, but two midwives refuse.
1.d: The midwives Shiphrah and Puah are named [[bible:Exodus 1:15]], while “Pharaoh” is a royal title, not a personal name [[nabre:exodus/1]]. Israel’s fruitfulness in 1:7 echoes the blessing of creation [[nabre:exodus/1]] [[bible:Genesis 1:28]].

2.s: A Hebrew mother hides her baby in a basket on the Nile; Pharaoh’s daughter finds him and names him Moses. Grown up, Moses kills an Egyptian, flees to Midian, and marries. God hears Israel’s groaning.
2.d: The word for the basket is the same Hebrew word as Noah’s ark, used nowhere else: as Noah was saved from the flood, Moses is saved from the Nile [[nabre:exodus/2]]. The name Moses is probably Egyptian, as in names like Thutmoses [[nabre:exodus/2]]. Hebrews 11:24–27 reflects on his choice to share his people’s suffering [[bible:Hebrews 11:24-27]].

3.s: God speaks to Moses from a burning bush that is not consumed, sends him to free Israel, and reveals his name: “I AM WHO I AM”, Yahweh.
3.d: “I AM” translates the Hebrew ’ehyeh, “I am” or “I will be”, and the name Yahweh is linked to the verb “to be” [[nabre:exodus/3]]. Out of reverence Jews later said Adonai, “Lord”, instead of the name; “Jehovah” comes from a misreading [[nabre:exodus/3]]. Jesus says, “before Abraham came into existence, I AM” [[bible:John 8:58]].

4.s: Moses protests he cannot speak well; God gives him signs and appoints his brother Aaron as his spokesman. Moses returns to Egypt, and the people believe.
4.d: God calls Israel “my firstborn” and warns Pharaoh about his own firstborn, the background to the final plague [[bible:Exodus 4:22-23]]. The night attack in 4:24–26 “continues to perplex commentators” [[nabre:exodus/4]]. God hardening Pharaoh’s heart “does not diminish Pharaoh’s own responsibility” [[nabre:exodus/4]].

5.s: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let the people go; he refuses and makes them gather their own straw for bricks. The people blame Moses.
5.d: Pharaoh asks, “Who is Yahweh?” [[bible:Exodus 5:2]], refusing to acknowledge the LORD’s authority [[nabre:exodus/5]]. His order begins “This is what Pharaoh says”, the formula prophets use for God’s word, here spoken by Pharaoh [[nabre:exodus/5]].

6.s: God renews his promise: “I will take you to myself for a people. I will be your God” The family tree of Moses and Aaron is given.
6.d: This chapter retells the call of Moses from chapters 3–4 in the words of the Priestly tradition [[nabre:exodus/6]]. God says he was not known to the patriarchs by the name Yahweh; the emphasis is on understanding God through his name [[nabre:exodus/6]].

7.s: Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent, and the first plague turns the Nile to blood, but Pharaoh’s heart is hardened.
7.d: The plagues run from 7:14 to 12:30. Some can be read as natural events, but the book presents them as extraordinary acts of God, coming exactly when Moses announces them [[nabre:exodus/7]]. In the end the LORD says he will judge “all the gods of Egypt” [[bible:Exodus 12:12]]. Paul discusses the hardening of Pharaoh in Romans 9 [[bible:Romans 9:17-18]].

8.s: Plagues of frogs, gnats and flies. Pharaoh promises to let the people go, then changes his mind.
8.d: For the first time Egypt’s magicians cannot match the sign and say, “This is God’s finger” [[nabre:exodus/8]] [[bible:Exodus 8:19]]. Jesus uses the same phrase of his own power over demons [[bible:Luke 11:20]]. From the flies onward Israel is set apart from Egypt [[nabre:exodus/8]] [[bible:Exodus 8:22-23]].

9.s: Plagues on livestock, boils and hail. Pharaoh admits he has sinned, but hardens his heart again.
9.d: The exact nature of the boils is not clear; the Hebrew suggests an inflammation [[nabre:exodus/9]]. God says he raised up Pharaoh “to show you my power” [[bible:Exodus 9:16]], a verse Paul quotes [[bible:Romans 9:17]]. The Hebrew word for the thunder is literally “voices of God” [[nabre:exodus/9]].

10.s: Locusts strip the land and darkness covers Egypt for three days, while the Israelites have light. Pharaoh refuses to let the flocks go.
10.d: Some commentators link the darkness to the hot desert sandstorm called the khamsin, but the book presents it as extraordinary [[nabre:exodus/10]]. The “Red Sea” of 10:19 is in Hebrew the “Sea of Reeds” [[nabre:exodus/10]]. Only Israel’s homes have light [[bible:Exodus 10:23]].

11.s: God warns of the last plague: every firstborn in Egypt will die.
11.d: The last plague answers Pharaoh’s refusal to release Israel, God’s “firstborn” [[bible:Exodus 4:22-23]], and his order to kill Hebrew boys [[bible:Exodus 1:22]]. Even so, God says, Israel will leave with the Egyptians’ favour [[bible:Exodus 11:2-3]].

12.s: The first Passover: each family kills a lamb and puts its blood on the doorframe so the plague passes over them. At midnight Egypt’s firstborn die, and Pharaoh sends Israel out.
12.d: Passover begins a new calendar for Israel [[nabre:exodus/12]] and becomes its yearly memorial [[bible:Exodus 12:14]]. Christians read the Passover lamb as “a prophetic type of Christ”: John applies 12:46, “Do not break any of its bones”, to Jesus on the cross [[nabre:exodus/12]] [[bible:John 19:36]], and Paul calls Christ “our Passover” [[bible:1 Corinthians 5:7]].

13.s: The firstborn of Israel are dedicated to God, and the feast of unleavened bread is set. God leads the people by a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Joseph’s bones go with them.
13.d: The pillar of cloud by day and fire by night is probably a single phenomenon [[nabre:exodus/13]]; the same cloud later covers the tabernacle [[bible:Exodus 40:34-38]]. Jewish tradition based the phylacteries (tefillin) on 13:9 [[nabre:exodus/13]].

14.s: Pharaoh’s army chases Israel to the sea. Moses says, “Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh”; the waters part, Israel crosses on dry ground, and the Egyptians drown.
14.d: The places named in 14:2 have not been identified with certainty [[nabre:exodus/14]]. The “Red Sea” is literally the “Sea of Reeds”, likely shallow water north of today’s Red Sea [[nabre:exodus/10]] [[nabre:exodus/15]]. Paul calls the crossing a kind of baptism [[bible:1 Corinthians 10:1-2]].

15.s: Moses and Miriam lead Israel in a song of victory. In the desert the water at Marah is bitter until God makes it sweet.
15.d: Many scholars regard the Song of the Sea as one of the oldest compositions in the Bible [[nabre:exodus/15]]. Miriam’s refrain repeats its first line as an answering chorus [[nabre:exodus/15]]. Revelation has the redeemed singing “the song of Moses … and the song of the Lamb” [[bible:Revelation 15:3]].

16.s: The hungry people grumble, and God sends quail and manna, bread from heaven, each morning, with a double portion before the Sabbath.
16.d: “Manna” is explained by the question man hu, “What is it?” [[nabre:exodus/16]]. It may be compared to a resin still found in Sinai, yet the book presents it as a sign of God’s care [[nabre:exodus/16]]. Christian tradition sees it as a type of the Eucharist, as Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven [[nabre:exodus/16]] [[bible:John 6:31-35]].

17.s: Water comes from the rock at Horeb. Israel defeats the Amalekites while Moses’s arms are held up by Aaron and Hur.
17.d: Massah means “place of the test” and Meribah “place of strife” [[nabre:exodus/17]], recalled in Psalm 95 [[bible:Psalm 95:8-9]]. Paul says of the rock that followed Israel, “the rock was Christ” [[bible:1 Corinthians 10:4]]. Moses names the altar “Yahweh our Banner” [[nabre:exodus/17]].

18.s: Moses’s father-in-law Jethro visits and advises him to share the work of judging the people with capable leaders.
18.d: Jethro, priest of Midian, was probably already a worshipper of the LORD [[nabre:exodus/18]]. His advice shapes Israel’s system of judges [[nabre:exodus/18]] [[bible:Exodus 18:21-22]].

19.s: At Mount Sinai God offers a covenant: Israel will be his treasured possession, “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation”. The mountain shakes with thunder, fire and smoke.
19.d: Israel camps at Sinai from here to Numbers 10, showing how central Sinai is [[nabre:exodus/19]]. The whole nation is set apart as “a kingdom of priests” [[nabre:exodus/19]], titles that 1 Peter applies to the church [[bible:1 Peter 2:9]]. Hebrews contrasts fearful Sinai with joyful Mount Zion [[bible:Hebrews 12:18-24]].

20.s: God speaks the Ten Commandments to all the people, beginning, “I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” The people are afraid and ask Moses to speak to them instead.
20.d: The commandments open with what God has done: “who brought you out of the land of Egypt” [[bible:Exodus 20:2]]. Jews, Catholics and Lutherans, and the Orthodox and Reformed divide the ten slightly differently [[ref:ewtn-decalogue]]. The list is repeated in Deuteronomy 5 [[bible:Deuteronomy 5:6-21]].

21.s: Laws about servants, violence, injuries and property, including “eye for eye, tooth for tooth”.
21.d: These laws have parallels in other ancient Near Eastern law codes [[nabre:exodus/21]]. The limits on slavery lessen its harms, though slavery itself is not condemned in the Old Testament [[nabre:exodus/21]]. “Eye for eye” expresses rigorous accountability; whether it was ever applied literally is debated, and Jesus calls for a deeper justice [[nabre:exodus/21]] [[bible:Matthew 5:38-42]].

22.s: Laws on theft, damage, and care for the vulnerable: do not mistreat foreigners, widows or orphans, “for you were aliens in the land of Egypt”.
22.d: Foreigners, widows and orphans must not be wronged, “for you were aliens in the land of Egypt” [[bible:Exodus 22:21-22]]. Israel’s own memory of slavery is the reason given for compassion, as again in 23:9 [[bible:Exodus 23:9]].

23.s: Laws of justice and the three yearly feasts. God promises his angel will lead Israel into the land.
23.d: The three yearly feasts are Passover and Unleavened Bread, Weeks, and Booths [[nabre:exodus/23]]. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk” is the basis of the Jewish separation of meat and dairy [[nabre:exodus/23]]. Justice reaches enemies too: help even your enemy’s straying donkey [[bible:Exodus 23:4-5]].

24.s: Israel agrees to the covenant, and Moses sprinkles “the blood of the covenant” on the people. The elders see God and eat before him; Moses goes up the mountain for forty days.
24.d: The twelve pillars stand for the twelve tribes entering the covenant [[nabre:exodus/24]]. The elders see God and live, and share a sacrificial meal [[nabre:exodus/24]]. Jesus’s words “my blood of the new covenant” echo 24:8 [[bible:Mark 14:24]], and Hebrews discusses the scene [[bible:Hebrews 9:18-20]].

25.s: God asks for gifts to build a sanctuary “that I may dwell among them”, and gives the design of the ark, the table and the lampstand.
25.d: The ark’s cover, the “mercy seat”, is linked to the Hebrew word for atonement, and its cherubim, probably winged lions with human heads, form a throne for the invisible LORD [[nabre:exodus/25]]. The lampstand, the menorah, is still used in Jewish worship today [[nabre:exodus/25]]. Hebrews says the tabernacle copied a heavenly pattern [[bible:Hebrews 8:5]].

26.s: Instructions for the tabernacle’s curtains, frames and the veil that separates the Most Holy Place.
26.d: The inner veil before the Most Holy Place is woven with cherubim, while the entrance curtain is not [[nabre:exodus/26]] [[bible:Exodus 26:31-36]]. When Jesus died the temple veil was torn in two [[bible:Matthew 27:51]].

27.s: Instructions for the bronze altar, the courtyard and the oil for the lamp.
27.d: The altar’s horns stand for strength and dignity and mark its sacred character [[nabre:exodus/27]]. It is a hollow box, probably filled with earth or stones when in use [[nabre:exodus/27]].

28.s: Garments for Aaron and his sons: the ephod, the breastpiece with twelve stones for the tribes, and a gold plate reading “Holy to Yahweh”.
28.d: The skilled workers are “wise-hearted”: in the Bible, wisdom includes practical skill [[nabre:exodus/28]]. The breastpiece holds the Urim and Thummim, lots used to learn God’s decision [[nabre:exodus/28]]. Aaron carries the tribes’ names on his shoulders and over his heart before the LORD [[bible:Exodus 28:12]] [[bible:Exodus 28:29]].

29.s: The ceremony to ordain Aaron and his sons as priests, and the daily morning and evening offerings.
29.d: The goal of the whole rescue is stated here: “I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will be their God” [[bible:Exodus 29:45-46]].

30.s: The altar of incense, the atonement money, the bronze basin, the anointing oil and the holy incense.
30.d: Incense later becomes a picture of prayer [[bible:Psalm 141:2]] [[bible:Revelation 8:3-4]].

31.s: God fills Bezalel with his Spirit to craft the tabernacle, and gives the Sabbath as a sign. Moses receives the two stone tablets.
31.d: God has “called by name” Bezalel and filled him with his Spirit for craftsmanship [[nabre:exodus/31]] [[bible:Exodus 31:2-3]]. The Sabbath is “a sign between me and you” [[bible:Exodus 31:13]].

32.s: While Moses is on the mountain the people make a golden calf and worship it. Moses breaks the tablets, the Levites punish the idolaters, and Moses pleads for the people.
32.d: The calf was probably meant as an image of the LORD himself, not of another god [[nabre:exodus/32]]; Jeroboam later sets up calves at Bethel and Dan with almost the same words [[bible:1 Kings 12:28]]. God relenting after Moses’ plea is a testimony to Israel’s belief in the power of intercessory prayer [[nabre:exodus/32]].

33.s: God says he will not go with them, but Moses pleads, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here.” He asks to see God’s glory and is shown God’s back.
33.d: The LORD knows Moses “by name”, as an intimate friend [[nabre:exodus/33]]. “My face” means God’s presence; tradition held that seeing God brought death [[nabre:exodus/33]] [[bible:Exodus 33:20]].

34.s: God renews the covenant and proclaims his name: “merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth”. Moses’s face shines.
34.d: 34:6 is an often-repeated statement of belief in Israel, echoed in Numbers, the Psalms, Joel and Jonah [[nabre:exodus/34]] [[bible:Jonah 4:2]]. The Hebrew for Moses’ “shining” face is spelled like “horns”, the origin of horned Moses in art [[nabre:exodus/34]]. Paul reflects on the veil over his face [[bible:2 Corinthians 3:12-18]].

35.s: The people bring gifts so generous that they must be told to stop, and the work begins.
35.d: The people give so generously that they must be told to stop [[bible:Exodus 36:5-7]]. Chapters 35–40 belong to the Priestly material describing Israel’s worship [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].

36.s: The craftsmen make the curtains and frames of the tabernacle.
36.d: The making of the tabernacle follows the instructions of chapter 26 point by point [[nabre:exodus/36]] [[bible:Exodus 26:1-37]].

37.s: Bezalel makes the ark, the table, the lampstand and the altar of incense.
37.d: Bezalel makes the ark, table, lampstand and incense altar exactly as they were described in chapters 25 and 30 [[nabre:exodus/37]].

38.s: The bronze altar, the basin and the courtyard are made, with an account of the metals used.
38.d: The ancient mirrors given for the basin were usually of polished bronze [[nabre:exodus/38]]. The women serving at the entrance appear again in 1 Samuel 2:22 [[bible:1 Samuel 2:22]].

39.s: The priests’ garments are made, and Moses inspects the finished work and blesses the people.
39.d: “As Yahweh commanded Moses” sounds again and again [[bible:Exodus 39:1]] [[bible:Exodus 39:43]], and Moses blesses them when the work is finished [[bible:Exodus 39:43]].

40.s: The tabernacle is set up, and the cloud covers it and the glory of Yahweh fills it, so that even Moses cannot enter.
40.d: The tabernacle is set up almost a year after Israel left Egypt [[nabre:exodus/40]]. The book ends with God’s glory living among his people [[bible:Exodus 40:34-38]]. John says the Word “lived among us” [[bible:John 1:14]].
